Research problem: Can MVFA's segmentation adapters be trained without any pixel masks, using only image-level normal/abnormal labels on all six BMAD source datasets, by replacing the Dice + Focal targets with pseudo-masks derived from the frozen CLIP patch features (patches of an abnormal training image that have no close neighbour among the patches of normal images of the same dataset), and how much of the zero-shot pixel-level AUROC and Dice of the mask-supervised MVFA does this recover on a held-out modality?
Rationale: MVFA's anomaly maps come only from the segmentation adapters, which are trained with Dice and Focal losses on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC masks (G3); the three image-only datasets (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS) never contribute localisation supervision, and the few-shot setting additionally assumes K masked abnormal images (G4). The related work shows that weaker signals can supervise localisation: CoDeGraph [30] filters consistent anomalies with batch-level patch graphs and shows that the resulting pseudo-masks can supervise prompt-driven vision-language models; DDAD [54] exploits unlabelled abnormal images alongside normal ones; MediCLIP [10] and SpatioPrompt [20] adapt CLIP from normal images with synthetic anomalies; MedSAD-CLIP [8] instead assumes real masks. None of these tests whether MVFA's multi-level residual adapters, the target method's own component, can be trained from image-level labels alone. The question is fine-grained (one loss target of one branch), feasible on BMAD with one GPU because pseudo-masks are computed once with frozen features, and measurable under the shared protocol: pixel AUROC and Dice on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC when held out, compared with the re-run mask-supervised MVFA, plus the effect of adding the three mask-free datasets as localisation sources. A positive answer removes MVFA's dependence on dense expert masks; a negative one quantifies how much masks are worth.

The risk is pseudo-mask quality on low-contrast modalities (ChestXray, HIS), which could make the comparison uninformative. Feedback: Report results as a label-cost curve (no masks, masks on one dataset, masks on three) to make the significance concrete.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G3. Localisation supervision requires dense masks: MVFA trains two branches. The detection (classification) adapters receive an image-level BCE loss on every source image, including the three BMAD datasets that have no masks (OCT17, ChestXray, HIS). The segmentation adapters, which produce the anomaly maps, are trained only with Dice and Focal losses on pixel-level masks, i.e. only on BrainMRI, LiverCT and RESC. Localisation therefore depends entirely on dense expert masks from three datasets; no image-level, sparse or normal-only supervision of the segmentation branch is formulated.
- G4. The few-shot setting needs labelled abnormal images with masks and is evaluated on one draw: In the released code, 'K-shot' means K normal AND K abnormal images, the abnormal ones with pixel masks, both drawn from BMAD's valid/ split; the adapters are fine-tuned on them per target task. Clinical few-shot supervision may instead contain only normal or unlabelled images, which the method does not support. Only one fixed draw per dataset is provided. Training time and compute for the per-task fine-tuning are not reported.

No new clinical data can be collected and no new expert annotations can be made.
- Shared evaluation protocol (from limitation group C: G2, G10, G12, G16): checkpoints and hyper-parameters are selected on a held-out validation split of the SOURCE modalities and never on the target test set, and the MVFA baseline is re-run under the same rule; results are reported under a modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out split (RESC and OCT17 are held out together, never one with the other in training), with patient-level separation where identifiers exist, over at least 3 random seeds and 3 few-shot support draws with mean and standard deviation, and against the missing baselines named in G12 where relevant.
